Q: Knapsack variant problem with topN solutions of fixed size A:

It's possible to write a non-brute-force solution using iterated LP. It isn't enough to impose a moving constraint on the value objective, though, because that will eliminate duplicates (which I assume you want to keep). That means that you also need to impose assignment variable ordering though e.g. exponential weights:

import functools

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import LinearConstraint, milp, Bounds


def solve_all(
    items: tuple[tuple[float, float]],  # value, weight
    max_weight: float,
    top_n: int, n_items: int | None = None,
):
    n = len(items)

    sol_constraints = ()
    weight = np.array([weight for value, weight in items])
    weight_constraint = LinearConstraint(A=weight, ub=max_weight)
    base_constraints = (weight_constraint,)
    if n_items is not None:
        item_constraint = LinearConstraint(A=np.ones(n), lb=n_items, ub=n_items)
        base_constraints += (item_constraint,)

    order_cost = 2.**np.arange(-1, -1-n, -1)
    value_cost = np.array([value for value, weight in items])
    cost = order_cost - value_cost

    curried = functools.partial(
        milp, c=cost,
        integrality=np.ones(shape=n, dtype=np.int8),
        bounds=Bounds(lb=np.zeros(n), ub=np.ones(n)))

    for _ in range(top_n):
        result = curried(constraints=base_constraints + sol_constraints)
        if not result.success:
            return
        yield result.x > 0.5, result.x @ value_cost, result.x @ weight
        order_constraint = LinearConstraint(A=cost, lb=result.fun + order_cost[-1])
        sol_constraints = (order_constraint,)


def main() -> None:
    items = ((4, 12), (2, 1), (6, 4), (1, 1), (2, 2))
    for selects, value, weight in solve_all(items, max_weight=15,  # n_items=4,
                                            top_n=3):
        print(f'value={value} weight={weight} selected={selects.astype(int)}')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Q: Fuzzy Matching Optimization in PySpark A:

One option that hasn’t been mentioned yet, and that fits this A→B matching pattern really well, is the /reconcile endpoint of Similarity API.

You provide the two columns/lists (A = Name1, B = Name2) and it returns the best match(es) from B for each value in A. You can set a bunch of parameters (but I think those are optional):

  • top_n = 1 to return only the single best match per Name1 (or increase it for top-k),

  • a similarity threshold to keep only matches above a chosen score,

  • optional preprocessing/normalization options and output format.

import requests

url = "https://api.similarity-api.com/reconcile"
headers = {
    "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_SIMILARITY_API_KEY",
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
}

payload = {
    "data_a": ["Microsoft", "appLE"],
    "data_b": ["Apple Inc.", "Microsoft"],
    "config": {"top_n": 1, "similarity_threshold": 0.75},
}

resp = requests.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload, timeout=60)
resp.raise_for_status()
print(resp.json())

full docs page here: https://similarity-api.com/documentation

Under the hood it’s built to avoid the full cartesian product by doing candidate generation/blocking + scoring efficiently, so it’s designed to handle large datasets (like, millions of records) without you having to implement blocking logic in Spark or wherever you decide to use it.

Caveat is that it is a paid service, so it’s mainly attractive if you have budget (tho it is often cheaper than burning a lot of cluster time on cross joins + Python UDFs). There’s also a free trial and a web UI, so you can test it quickly on a sample or even run a full job if it fits within the trial limits.

Q: constructing a vector of object using std::initializer_list A:

You attempt to create a vector of Cols from an initializer list of std::strings. There's no conversion from std::initializer_list<std::string> to a std::initializer_list<Col> even though there is a conversion from std::string to Col. Thats the reason using the iterator constructor works (conversion from std::string to Col) but not the one taking the initializer list.

Generally speaking, there is no implicit relation between X<T> and X<U> other than being instantiations of X. For example there is also no direct conversion from std::vector<std::string> to std::vector<Col> (while you can construct a std::vector<Col> with iterators to the vector of strings).

Q: No paste event when shift key is down in Firefox A:

This can be solved by setting the contenteditable attribute to true for the element which has the focus.

Q: Swift JSONDecode decoding arrays fails if single element decoding fails A:

Instead, You can also do like this:

struct GroceryProduct: Decodable {
    var name: String
    var points: Int
    var description: String?
}

and then in while getting it:

let groceryList = try JSONDecoder().decode(Array<GroceryProduct>.self, from: responseData)
